rows.evidence: Q1: Methods 2.1-2.2 and Results 3.2-3.3 report the authors' own four-year field deployment of infrared radiometers, weather and soil sensors at two commercial Idaho vineyards, with CWSI correlated against measured LWP and fASW.
rows.notes: The study uses point in-situ infrared radiometers (thermal sensors) to compute a daily CWSI that was significantly correlated with LWP and fASW (Fig. 7) and was used by managers for irrigation decisions. It does not identify spatial water-stress zones (point sensors on a single row) and reports no yield or grape-quality data, so the crop_production effect (maintaining yield and quality) is not tested. Only the precondition (stress detection and irrigation guidance) is shown.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own sensor deployment, CWSI calculation with weather inputs, and correlation with LWP and fASW over four seasons.
rows.notes: The study integrates CWSI with in-situ thermal radiometers (not thermal imagery) and real-time weather data, and shows CWSI tracked vine water status and guided irrigation. No stress-zone mapping and no yield or quality measurements are reported, so the claimed effect of preserving grape quality and yield is not evidenced; the study supports only the upstream step of stress monitoring and irrigation guidance.

rows.evidence: Q1: Own field data, Tables 1-2 and Figs. 7-8, from two Idaho vineyards over 2017-2020.
rows.notes: The study is in Idaho, not Chile, and uses wired radiometers with a cellular-modem data logger rather than a WSN; reference temperatures come from a neural network plus an energy-balance equation. It reports seasonal irrigation amounts (Table 2) that were consistent across years but gives no baseline comparison and no water-savings figure (no 25% or any percentage). Water conservation is therefore not evidenced; the DSS-based scheduling is at most a precondition.

rows.evidence: Q1: Own field deployment and measurements reported in Sections 2-3.
rows.notes: No grape quality parameters (sugar, acidity) or yield were measured in this study; it reports only vine water status indicators (CWSI, LWP, fASW) and irrigation amounts. Location and system description in the passage (Chile, WSN) also do not match this Idaho IoT study. The study supports only the upstream step of scheduling irrigation to a target stress level.

rows.evidence: Q1: Own four-year field deployment (Sections 2-3). Q2: Table 2 and Section 4.4 report that seasonal average daily CWSI (0.23-0.31 at V-A, 0.36-0.44 at V-B) and cumulative irrigation were kept consistent in 2018-2020 despite year-to-year differences in evaporative demand and precipitation (Table 1), which the authors interpret as managers effectively using the DSS to maintain a consistent deficit irrigation program. Q4: Fig. 7 and Fig. 8 measure the intermediate variable, vine water status (CWSI validated against pressure-chamber LWP and sensor-based fASW), and show irrigation events lowering CWSI and raising fASW. Q6: Section 2.1 and 4.4 report the effect at the level of two commercial estate vineyards (<7 ha) whose managers scheduled whole-vineyard irrigation using the DSS. Q7: Section 4.5 states from own data that solar radiation below 200 W m-2 and wet canopies produced invalid CWSI values, that the models are valid only for wind speeds within the calibration range (<5 m s-1) and semiarid conditions, and that managers were briefed on CWSI interpretation. Q8: Section 4.5 states limits: two small vineyards in one semiarid region, models may not transfer to other climates, expensive equipment, LWP sometimes measured on different vines and under variable clouds.
rows.notes: The study supports the resilience part of the claim (consistent vine water stress and irrigation across climatically different years) but reports no productivity data. Q3 no: the cross-year consistency rests on CWSI and irrigation records only; LWP/fASW validate the index rather than the adaptation result. Q5 no: two sites, two soils, one climate region; cultivars are of one crop. Q9 no: Table 2 gives seasonal means without SD or CI; the only dispersion reported (Table 1) concerns 20-yr climate normals, not the claimed result.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a four-year deployment of an in-situ thermal CWSI IoT decision support system at two Idaho commercial vineyards; it measures vine water status and irrigation amounts but no yield, grape quality or water savings, and is not located in Chile nor based on a WSN as the review passages for rows 17-19 state.
